CHAPTER XVI

THE PRESS (1868)

At ten o'clock of a July night, in heat that made the tropical rain-shower simmer, the Adams family clambered down the side of their Cunard steamer into the government tugboat, which set them ashore in black darkness at the end of some North River pier. Had they been Tyrian traders of the year B.C. 1000 landing from a galley fresh from Gibraltar, they could hardly have been stranger on the shore of a world so changed from what it had been ten years before. Towards midnight they found shelter in their native land.

How much its character had changed they could not wholly know. Society in America was always trying, almost as blindly as an earthworm, to realize and understand itself; to catch up with its own head, and to twist about in search of its tail. It offered the profile of a long, straggling caravan, stretching loosely towards the prairies, its few score of leaders far in advance and its millions of immigrants, negroes, and Indians far in the rear, somewhere in archaic time. Each newcomer needed to slip into a place as near the head as possible, and needed most to know where the leaders could be found.

One could divine pretty nearly where the force lay. The last ten years had given to coal, iron, steam a distinct superiority over agriculture, handwork, and learning; but the result on a survivor from the fifties resembled the action of the earthworm; he twisted about, in vain, to recover his starting-point; he could no longer see his own trail; he had become an estray, a flotsam or jetsam of wreckage, a belated reveller, or a scholar-gipsy like Matthew Arnold's. His world was dead. Not a Polish Jew fresh from Warsaw or Cracow but had a keener instinct, an intenser energy, and a freer hand than he—American of Americans, with Heaven knew how many Puritans and Patriots behind him, and an education that had cost a civil war. He vehemently insisted that he was not himself at fault. He had been unfairly forced out of the track, and must get back into it as best he could.

Little as he might be fitted for the work before him, he had only to look at his father and Motley to see figures less fitted for it than he. All were equally survivals from the forties—bric-à-brac from the time of Louis Philippe; stylists; doctrinaires; ornaments more or less suited to colonial architecture, but of little value in Desbrosses Street or Fifth Avenue. The country needed ornament—needed it badly—but it needed energy still more, and capital most of all. To fit out an entire continent with roads and the decencies of life would exhaust the credit of the entire planet. The mere suggestion that a sun existed above him would outrage the self-respect of a deep-sea fish that carried a lantern on the end of its nose.

The new Americans, whether fit or unfit, must create a world of their own, a science, a society, a philosophy, a universe, where they had not yet created a road or even learned to dig their own iron. They had no time for thought; they saw nothing beyond their day's work, and intensely disliked being told what to do by men who took their ideas from the abstract theories of history, philosophy, or theology. The generation between 1865 and 1895 was already mortgaged to the railways, and no one knew it better than the generation itself.

Henry Adams reached Quincy ready for the new start. His brother Charles had determined to strike for the railroads; Henry was to strike for the press; and they hoped to play into each other's hands. They had great need, for they found no one else to play with. After discovering the worthlessness of a so-called education, they had still to discover the worthlessness of so-called social connection. He was for sale, in the open market. So were many of his friends. All the world knew it, and knew too that they were cheap—to be bought at the price of a mechanic. The labor market of good society was ill-organized.

Boston seemed to offer no market for educated labor. One no longer dined at two o'clock; one heard talk of Bostonians worth five millions or more as something not incredible. The less one meddled with the Boston press, the better. Boston meant business. The Bostonians were building railways. Adams would have liked to help in building railways, but had no education. He was not fit.

He passed three or four months visiting relations and studying the situation. At thirty years old, the man who has not yet got further than to study the situation, is lost, or near it. He went to Newport and tried to be fashionable, but failed as fashion. Society seemed founded on the law that all was for the best New Yorkers in the best of Newports, and that all young people were rich if they could waltz.

In thus sacrificing his heritage, he only followed the path that had led him from the beginning. He had reckoned from childhood on outlawry as his peculiar birthright. The mere thought of beginning life again in Mount Vernon Street lowered the pulsations of his heart. Neither by temperament nor by education was he fitted for Boston; he had to go.

He stuck to his plan of joining the press, and selected Washington as the shortest road to New York. In 1868, Washington stood outside the social pale. No Bostonian had ever gone there. One announced one's self as an adventurer and an office-seeker, a person of deplorably bad judgment, and the charges were true. That he must educate himself over again, for objects quite new, in an air altogether hostile to his old educations, was the only certainty. For large work he could count on the *North American Review*; for current discussion, on the New York *Nation*; but what he needed was a New York daily, and no New York daily needed him. The *Tribune*, the *Sun*, the *Herald* were each impossible for political, personal, or temperamental reasons—he must always fail as a blackguard. There remained only Bryant's *Evening Post* and Godkin's *Nation*, the same circle of readers he reached in the *North American*.

The outlook was dim, but at Washington he had the personal friendship of Mr. Evarts, then Attorney General. Evarts did what no one in Boston seemed to care for doing: he held out a hand to the young man. Generous by nature, prodigal in hospitality, fond of young people, a born man-of-the-world, he gave and took liberally, and accepted the world without fearing or abusing it. Kindness seldom came more happily than when Mr. Evarts took him to Washington in October, 1868.

Adams accepted the hospitality of the sleeper with deep gratitude, the more because his first struggle with a sleeping-car made him doubt the value—to him—of a Pullman civilization. He abode at Mr. Evarts's house in H Street till he found rooms in the roomless village. To him the village seemed unchanged. Had he not known that a great war and eight years of astonishing movement had passed over it, he would have noticed nothing that betrayed growth. As of old, houses were few; rooms fewer; even the men were the same. His best chance lay in the eighteenth century.

The first acquaintance was naturally the President. Evarts presented him at the White House to Andrew Johnson. The interview was brief and consisted in the stock remark common to monarchs and valets, that the young man looked even younger than he was. The younger man felt even younger than he looked. Yet musing on it long afterwards, he could not help recalling the President's figure with a distinctness that surprised him. The old-fashioned Southern Senator and statesman sat in his chair with a look of self-esteem that had its value. To them the universe was serious, even solemn, but it was their universe, a Southern conception of right. Lamar used to say that he never entertained a doubt of the soundness of the Southern system until he found that slavery could not stand a war. The life of it all—the vigor—the poetry—was its moral certainty of self. The Southerner could not doubt; and this self-assurance not only gave Andrew Johnson the look of a true President, but actually made him one. The Executive in 1868 was perhaps the strongest Adams was ever to see.

Seward was still Secretary of State, little changed. He was the same—with a difference. Perhaps he had at last got an education, and all he wanted; perhaps he had resigned himself to doing without it. He appeared to have closed his account with the public; he no longer seemed to care; he asked nothing, gave nothing, and waited only for his discharge. Wanting to feel that the only chief he ever served even as a volunteer recognized some personal relation, Adams asked Mr. Seward to dine with him one evening and play whist. Mr. Seward came and had his whist, and Adams remembered his rough parting speech: "A very sensible entertainment!"

The State Department had ceased to be the centre of his interest, and the Treasury had taken its place. There Adams found himself among the active and intelligent young men of the country—men from the army, with the spirit of the volunteers, eager for reform. The whole government, from top to bottom, was rotten with the senility of what was antiquated and the instability of what was improvised. The Civil War had made a new system in fact; the country would have to reorganize the machinery in practice and theory.

Just then the Supreme Court was about to take up the Legal Tender cases. Evarts was anxious to fix on a line of argument that should stand against Judge Curtis, the last of the strong jurists of Marshall's school, and deliberately forced discussion. Day after day, driving, dining, walking, he provoked Adams to dispute his positions. He needed an anvil, he said, to hammer his ideas on. Adams was flattered at being an anvil, which is, after all, more solid than the hammer; and contradicted with freedom. The dispute led him to seek light from the Chief Justice himself, and he grew intimate with Mr. Chase, whose position towards Legal Tender was awkward, since as Secretary of the Treasury he had been its author, and as Chief Justice became its enemy. He was willing enough to win an ally in the press who would tell his story as he wished it read.

Sooner or later, Adams one day met Charles Sumner on the street and instantly stopped to greet him. As though eight years of broken ties were the natural course of friendship, Sumner dropped back into the relation of hero to the school boy, and Adams enjoyed accepting it. He was thirty; Sumner fifty-seven. The renewal of broken relations is a nervous matter, and in this case it bristled with thorns, for Sumner's quarrel with Mr. Adams had not been the most delicate of his ruptured relations. To Sumner, Adams in Washington should have seemed more or less of a critic, perhaps a spy, certainly an intriguer or adventurer; a politician without party; a writer without principles; an office-seeker certain to beg for support. All this was, for his purposes, true. He was the more surprised to see Sumner invite a renewal of old relations, treat him almost confidentially, ask him to make a fourth at the pleasant little dinners on La Fayette Square, admit him to the Senator's study, and inform him of views, policy, and purposes sometimes more astounding than his curious gaps or lapses of omniscience.

On the whole, the relation was the queerest that Henry Adams ever kept up. He liked and admired Sumner, but thought his mind a pathological study. Sumner's mind had reached the calm of water which receives and reflects images without absorbing them; it contained nothing but itself. The images from without existed by courtesy until the mental surface was ruffled, but never became part of the thought. Henry Adams roused no emotion; if he had roused a disagreeable one, he would have ceased to exist. The mind would have mechanically rejected, as it had mechanically admitted him.

In 1868 these great authorities were the stock-in-trade of the newspaper business; the accumulated capital of a Silurian age. A few months or years more, and they were gone. La Fayette Square was society. Within a few hundred yards of Mr. Clark Mills's nursery monument to the equestrian seat of Andrew Jackson, one found all one's acquaintance as well as hotels, banks, markets and national government. Beyond the Square the country began. No rich or fashionable stranger had yet discovered the town. The happy village was innocent of a club. The value of real estate had not increased since 1800, and the pavements were more impassable than the mud. All this favored a young man who had come to make a name. In four-and-twenty hours he could know everybody; in two days everybody knew him.

After seven years' arduous and unsuccessful effort to explore the outskirts of London society, the Washington world offered an easy and delightful repose. When he looked round on the men he was to work with—or against—he had to admit that nine-tenths of his acquired education was useless, and the other tenth harmful. He would have to begin again from the beginning. The task was amusing. For the moment, politics had ceased to disturb social relations. All parties were mixed up and jumbled together in a sort of tidal slack-water. The Government resembled Adams himself in the matter of education. All that had gone before was useless, and some of it was worse.
